issues.legal_issue: A grant of a named village comprising the village lands, including its poramboke, is an estate for purposes of rent reduction where minor inams do not constitute a reservation by the grantor.
material_facts: The inam register recorded the dry lands and poramboke together as comprised in the grant of the named village.
The village’s poramboke included the village site, ponds, waterways, paths and saline land, and the register treated its entire extent as part of the grant.
The minor inams were of immemorial or earlier origin, or were created by the grantees; their existence did not show that the grantor had reserved land.
issues.conclusion: The village was an estate within the applicable definition, and the government’s rent-reduction notification was valid.
issues.legal_principle: The Rent Reduction Act applied to estates as defined by section 3(2) of the Madras Estates Land Act, including an inam village whose grant was made, confirmed or recognised by the Government. Under section 3(2)(d) and Explanation 1, a grant expressed to be of a named village could constitute an estate despite certain lands previously granted or reserved for communal purposes. The terms and extent of the grant are determined from the available grant records, including the Inam Fair Register. The Court relied on District Board, Tanjore v. Noor Md. (1952-2 Mad LJ 586; AIR 1953 SC 446) and Krishnaswami v. Perumal Goundan (AIR 1950 PC 105).

rule.if: rent_reduction_challenge and grant_of_named_village and entire_village_lands_in_grant and minor_inams_not_grantor_reservations

predicates.rent_reduction_challenge: The proceeding challenges the application of a rent-reduction regime to property on the ground that it is not a qualifying estate.
predicates.grant_of_named_village: The grant records show that the grant was expressed to be of a named village.
predicates.entire_village_lands_in_grant: The grant records treat the village lands, including the poramboke, as comprised in the grant.
predicates.minor_inams_not_grantor_reservations: Any minor inams were pre-existing or created by the grantees, rather than lands reserved by the grantor when making the village grant.

issues.definition: When a rent-reduction challenge concerns a named-village grant that includes the village lands and whose minor inams do not reflect grantor reservations, the village is an estate for rent-reduction purposes.

issues.legal_issue: Civil courts cannot redecide whether an inam village is an inam estate when legislation assigns that determination to a designated officer and appellate tribunal and makes their decisions binding.
material_facts: The legislation authorised a Settlement Officer to inquire and determine whether an inam village was an inam estate, provided for an appeal to a Tribunal, and made the Tribunal’s decision final and not challengeable in court.
The legislation also made the Settlement Officer’s decision binding where no appeal was taken.
The suit sought to have a civil court determine that the village was not an inam estate.
issues.conclusion: The civil court’s jurisdiction to decide whether an inam village is an inam estate was excluded; that question belonged to the statutory authorities.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 9 of the Civil Procedure Code, civil jurisdiction is presumed unless expressly or impliedly barred. The statutory scheme’s designated inquiry, appeal, finality and binding-effect provisions together impliedly exclude civil-court jurisdiction over whether an inam village is an inam estate, including where the officer’s decision is not appealed. The Court relied on Secretary of State v. Mask and Co. (67 IA 222; AIR 1940 PC 105) and Firm of Illuri Subbayya Chetty v. State of Andhra Pradesh (AIR 1964 SC 322) for the limited exception where fundamental statutory requirements or fundamental principles of judicial procedure are violated; no such issue was raised here.

rule.if: civil_suit_retries_inam_estate_status and designated_officer_determines_status and statutory_appeal_provided and decisions_made_binding

predicates.civil_suit_retries_inam_estate_status: A civil suit asks the court to decide whether a property that is treated as an inam village is an inam estate.
predicates.designated_officer_determines_status: The governing legal scheme assigns the determination of inam-estate status to a designated officer after an inquiry.
predicates.statutory_appeal_provided: The governing legal scheme provides an appeal from the officer’s determination to a designated tribunal.
predicates.decisions_made_binding: The governing legal scheme makes the tribunal’s decision final and makes the officer’s decision binding when no appeal is taken.

issues.definition: When a civil suit seeks to retry inam-estate status that a designated officer and appeal tribunal are assigned to determine through a binding process, the civil court cannot redecide that status.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory officer authorised to decide whether an inam village is an inam estate does not thereby receive exclusive authority to decide conclusively whether the property is an inam village at all.
material_facts: The legislation directed the Settlement Officer to determine whether any inam village was an inam estate, but did not authorise the officer to determine conclusively whether the property was an inam village.
The Court found, in considering the rent-reduction issue, that the property was an inam village.
issues.conclusion: Whether the property was an inam village was a preliminary condition to the statutory officer’s jurisdiction and could be questioned in an ordinary civil proceeding; the finding that this property was an inam village satisfied that condition in this case.
issues.legal_principle: The scope of an exclusive statutory tribunal’s jurisdiction depends on the statute’s purpose and scheme. Under section 9(1) of the Abolition Act, the officer’s assigned determination concerned whether an inam village was an inam estate; the existence of an inam village was an assumed preliminary fact, and the Act did not empower the officer to decide that fact conclusively. The Court endorsed Venkatanarasayya v. State of Madras (1952 ILR Mad 680; AIR 1953 Mad 60) on the distinction between the threshold question whether a grant comprises a village and the statutory question whether that village is an inam estate.

predicates.civil_proceeding_contests_village_status: A civil proceeding challenges whether the property is an inam village in the first place.
predicates.statutory_officer_authorised_only_to_cla: The statutory officer is authorised to decide whether an inam village qualifies as an inam estate.
predicates.no_final_authority_over_village_threshol: The governing legal scheme does not empower the officer to determine conclusively whether the property is an inam village.

issues.definition: When a civil proceeding disputes village status and the statutory officer has no final authority over that threshold question, the civil court may determine village status.

issues.legal_issue: A purported dismissal of an appeal by a tribunal lacking the statutorily required composition is invalid and leaves the appeal pending.
material_facts: The statutory tribunal was required to consist of three members.
The appeal from the Settlement Officer was heard and dismissed by only two members.
issues.conclusion: The purported dismissal was a nullity, leaving the appeal pending before the Tribunal; it did not displace the Settlement Officer’s determination or permit a civil court to decide the inam-estate question.
issues.legal_principle: Where a tribunal’s legally required composition is not met, its purported decision is invalid. The Court accepted the conclusion that an invalid dismissal leaves the appeal undisposed of, rather than automatically vacating the earlier determination. The Tribunal’s jurisdiction over the inam-estate question remained exclusive under the statutory scheme.

predicates.appeal_from_status_determination: An appeal is taken from an officer’s determination of the property’s statutory status.
predicates.tribunal_required_to_have_three_members: The governing legal scheme requires the appellate tribunal to consist of three members.
predicates.appeal_decided_by_only_two_members: Only two members of the tribunal heard and purported to dispose of the appeal.

issues.definition: When an appeal is decided by only two members despite a requirement for three, the purported dismissal is invalid and the appeal remains pending.
